newsitem.title: MACAU: Macau holds last poll before 1999 return to China.
newsitem.headline: Macau holds last poll before 1999 return to China.

text.p: Residents of Macau began casting their votes on Sunday in the territory's final elections under Portuguese rule, before it reverts to China in 1999.

A slow but steady trickle of voters braved intermittent squalls to vote early -- the narrow, cobbled inner city hustings now quiet in the aftermath of a cacophony of loudhailers, patriotic songs and campaign karaoke that had accompanied the final flurry of electioneering.
"I'm definitely out to vote early," said 21-year-old jewellery shop assistant Carl Leong, who as a first-time voter planned to throw his weight behind a candidate well-known to his family.
Only eight of the Legislative Assembly's 23 seats are being directly contested in Sunday's poll.
The remainder of the assembly, which will straddle the handover to China on December 20, 1999, are either indirectly elected or appointed by the governor.

Ruled by Portugal for almost five centuries, and like nearby Hong Kong, this tiny territory of 424,000 mainly ethnic Chinese is set to become an autonomous Special Administrative Region of China under Beijing's plan to reunify lost territories.
But while the enclave, a rocky outcrop nestled at the southern tip of China, seems to lack campaign issues, it has never lacked scandal.
Best known for its casinos, the territory has regularly hit the headlines for vice, violence and a wave of gangland bombings.
More recently, the 14-day election campaign has been dogged by rumours of bribery and vote-rigging.
Local papers have avidly reported unsubstantiated claims that behind a political facade of karaoke campaigns and dim sum parties is a sinister price tag.
Some groups had spent up to 20 million patacas (US$2.5 million) to buy votes, with residents paying up to 2,500 patacas (US$320) to register to vote, papers said.

The electoral system is only partly democratic. The 116,000 voters directly elect eight members of the assembly, while eight are indirectly elected by business, labour and community organisations, and seven are appointed by the governor.
A record 62 candidates are vying for the eight directly elected seats.
In stark contrast to the British colony of Hong Kong, which reverts to China two and a half years earlier next July 1, Macau's assembly is not fighting for its survival beyond the 1999 handover,
China plans to dismantle Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council and replace it with a provisional chamber, sparking cries of foul play from democrats and from Britain.
Beijing has given Macau's election process a nod of approval, not only allowing it to straddle the handover, but extending its four-year tenure to 2001.
